title: Orwell Has Become What He Despised
text:
“Orwell Saw This Coming” ran the headline, and if you didn’t read any further, you might agree. The president was whipping up hatred in elaborate rage-fueled rallies and plastering banners bearing his glowering, oversize face on government buildings. The National Guard was patrolling the streets of Washington. Officials in the recently renamed Department of War were bragging about extrajudicial killings. The national-security apparatus had divided the world into three zones of influence, strikingly similar to The Party’s Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia from 1984 . But none of that was the this in “Orwell Saw This Coming,” which ran in The Free Press in January. This was New York City’s new mayor. “It’s fair to say that George Orwell would have despised Zohran Mamdani,” the columnist Charles Lane argued. Trump was hardly mentioned.

 In 2026, if an American writer brings up Orwell, chances are high that their target is the left, not the right. Over the past decade, one of the strangest habits among right-wing intellectuals and pundits has been their use of Orwell to defend the rise of authoritarianism in the U.S. The reference is shockingly common . “If 1984 has a practical lesson, it is this: There is a world of difference between a despotism dedicated to the expansion of socialism through federal-government power and a despotism dedicated to dismantling it,” Nathan Schlueter wrote in 2017 in National Review . “The former suffocates; the latter, though not without its serious dangers, just might create room to breathe.” The most direct rebuttal to this absurdity is Orwell’s own: “My recent novel is NOT intended as an attack on Socialism or on the British Labour Party (of which I am a supporter),” he once wrote to a curious reader.

 Orwell was literally antifa. In Spain, he fought with the militia of the Workers’ Party of Marxist Unification. Barcelona has a square named after him, and not because he supported far-right authoritarians against academics and students, as many conservative intellectuals would seem to believe.

 [ From the May 2024 issue: What Orwell really feared ] 

 Let’s call them the Orwellian Trumpists. They could not have misunderstood the writer, or the current political reality, any more thoroughly. To a certain extent, Orwell saw this coming. The dumbest mistakes are typically made by the intelligentsia, he once cautioned: “No ordinary man could be such a fool.” He has now become the subject of his own warning.

 Orwell transcends right and left in this sense: Everyone who writes a political opinion in English, whatever their persuasion, is following in his tradition. “Why I Write” and “Politics and the English Language” are the foundational texts of magazine and newspaper writing to this day. His style is so hard to replicate because it is so basic. Reading Orwell is like hearing a man say what he means. It’s an astonishingly difficult effect to imitate. I’m trying to write like him now. Almost every opinion writer you can name is trying to write like him too.

 The roots of right-wing Orwell worship are not hard to see when you consider his obsession with prose style and the debasement of political language. Orwell believed in political writing more than any other writer; he gave it a grandeur and a sense of purpose that play to the vanities of every opinion columnist. He believed in clarity, not just freedom of speech. Staleness, imprecision, and pretension were, for him, far more than technical flaws. They were signs of the onset of dehumanization.

 Over the past decade, as the banalities of identity politics entered academia and journalism, Orwell became an ideal lens by which to witness and critique the process. The left’s attempt to impose a new linguistic order by force of shame was, in fact, an attempt to repress the human.

 But the problem with today’s right-wing Orwellians is that they are living in the past. Trumpism is a far greater threat to the values Orwell fought for than wokeness ever could be. “The Orwellian Big Brother punishing you for expressing an impolitic thought is now the law of the land in the land of Orwell,” Rupa Subramanya, another writer for The Free Press , told a congressional committee last year. She said this while the Republican Party was detaining students for signing op-eds, and policing the border by looking for inappropriate social-media posts. DOGE, meanwhile, was pulling funding from government agencies on the basis of keyword searches.

 Everyone who has ever argued that the most significant threat to the Western canon comes from the left will need to reckon with the fact that Republicans were the ones who told professors to pull passages from Plato from a course at Texas A&M. It was Republicans who threw CDC data sets and significant chunks of the National Archives into a memory hole. Trump’s decrees about language have gone further than any Democrat ever dared: He changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Lake Ontario, to his obedient followers, is Lake America.

 The Orwellian Trumpists’ claims to support linguistic freedom are laughable, or beside the point. In their bitter partisanship, they resemble the neoconservatives of a previous era, the liberals mugged by reality. They lack the dignity of their predecessors, though. They’ve been mugged by reality television. I think of them as the Otto intellectuals: Otto is the character from the 1980s British comedy A Fish Called Wanda who thinks that Aristotle was Belgian and that the central message of Buddhism is every man for himself.

 The contortions of the Orwellian Trumpists would dazzle any Soviet apparatchik. The British historian Niall Ferguson, who has used Orwell’s line that “to see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle” on multiple occasions, has frequently sane-washed Trump’s foreign policy. In an episode of the Hoover Institution’s podcast GoodFellows about Trump’s “coercive diplomacy,” Ferguson claimed that Trump’s destruction of America’s alliances and his sprawling, pointless violence were the result of deep strategic thinking. If you’re arguing in favor of “coercive diplomacy,” a phrase precisely as meaningful as “violent seduction,” you’re not George Orwell. You’re closer to Lord Haw-Haw.

 Sometimes, as with the right-wing activist Christopher Rufo, using Orwell has explicitly partisan purposes. “What happens is that the left will say, ‘Well you’re opposing DEI; you don’t like diversity, you don’t like equity, you don’t like inclusion,’” Rufo said on his YouTube channel. “And you can say no, those are false words, those are Orwellian terms.” Citing Orwell becomes a technique in such cases, although aimed at a negligible slice of the political sphere: people who have heard the word Orwellian but have never bothered to think through what it means.

 [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The right is changing the rules of the culture war ] 

 As Orwell wrote in “Politics and the English Language,” he hated any argument that “consists in gumming together long strips of words which have already been set in order by someone else, and making the results presentable by sheer humbug.” Orwell has become what he most despised. He has set the strips of words in order, and someone else is gumming them together by sheer humbug. He’s jargon now. He’s the jargon for the supposedly anti-jargon crowd.

 Orwell’s contradictory status reminds me of his magnificent essay on Charles Dickens. Orwell is as distant from us today as Dickens was from Orwell. He was trying to understand how Dickens could be appropriated by people he would obviously have despised. “Dickens attacked English institutions with a ferocity that has never since been approached,” Orwell wrote. “Yet he managed to do it without making himself hated, and, more than this, the very people he attacked have swallowed him so completely that he has become a national institution himself.” The audience remembered his sentimentality. The actual import of his writing vanished.

 Dickens was critical of virtually every entrenched system in English life but even more critical of the attempts to overturn those systems. Tradition was brutality; revolution was terror. Dickens walked a line between “attacking everybody and antagonizing nobody,” Orwell wrote. In the end, Orwell could not suppress his adulation for the contradiction, for the refusal to fit in: Dickens was “a type hated with equal hatred by all the smelly little orthodoxies which are now contending for our souls,” he wrote. Those orthodoxies, unable to face Dickens’s recognition of their own fraudulence but unable to reject him because of the power of his writing, turned him into a vibe. The Dickens vibe remains in place today: squalid London, Christmas, cheekiness, wretched children.

 Orwell is being turned into a vibe just as Dickens before him. He is English to the fingertips: late-imperial, pre-multicultural, pubs with barmaids who call you “dearie,” memorized passages of Kipling, bad food, warm beer, and floggings in public schools—combined with a staunch criticism of every bit of that. Orwell was an Eton graduate who nonetheless described the upper classes as drunken, violent buffoons who were tolerable only at the moment they were being shot. At the same time, he was a committed leftist who became a critic of the totalitarian left as it took power across various states in the middle of the 20th century. The Orwell vibe is “aren’t English people clever?” meets “internal critic of the left.” As with Dickens, the vibe is half correct, half oblivious.

 The reason Orwell is such a paragon—the reason you can still feel the power of his writing long after every politician he mentioned is dead—is that he remained a party of one, even when he was shooting people or elephants, even when highly civilized human beings were flying overhead , trying to kill him. Now he exists through his contradictions: an Englishman who saw the brutality of England and yet remained English, a leftist who faced the brutality of communism and yet remained a leftist. “The words of a dead man are modified in the guts of the living,” as W. H. Auden said about Yeats. You can do what you like with Orwell’s words now.

 The Orwellian Trumpists have used their purported idol to justify a president who demands his followers accept obvious lies, who runs the government according to a standard of personal loyalty, who campaigns on two-minute hate, who revels in suspending the rules of war, who tears children from their mothers, who pardons for a fee, who has done everything in his power to separate language from meaning in order to camouflage his own brutality. They find themselves in an untenable position: Either they wanted all this or they have to admit that they got suckered by the most obvious con man in the history of con men.

 Perhaps it was inevitable that Orwell would devolve into just another vibe. But it’s shameful what that vibe turned out to be; the Orwellian Trumpists have chosen a boot stamping on a human face. It remains true that to see what’s in front of one’s nose requires a constant struggle.
